channel.title: balzac blog
channel.description: Short portraits of writers and composers.

item.title: Balzac, a whole society in ninety books
item.description:
Honoré de Balzac was born in Tours in 1799 and died in Paris in 1850. In about twenty years of work he wrote some ninety novels and stories, which he gathered under one title: La Comédie humaine.

Characters who come back

The idea that holds the whole together arrived with Le Père Goriot, in 1835. Balzac decided that a character met in one book could walk into another. Rastignac, a penniless student in that novel, is a minister later on. Vautrin, the convict, turns up again under other names.

Read in sequence, the books stop being separate stories. They become one city, where you keep running into people you already know.

Nights, coffee and proofs

Balzac wrote at night, for hours on end, with a great deal of coffee. He then rewrote on the printer's proofs, filling the margins until the page had to be set again. His printers dreaded him, and his debts followed him all his life.

He married Ewelina Hańska, the Polish countess he had been writing to for almost twenty years, in March 1850. He died five months later.

Why the name

A generator that turns plain text files into a whole site seemed a fair thing to name after him. Its development server listens on port 1799.

item.title: Dumas and the serial novel
item.description:
Alexandre Dumas was born in 1802 in Villers-Cotterêts, north-east of Paris. His father, Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, was born in Saint-Domingue to an enslaved woman and a French nobleman, and rose to the rank of general in the armies of the Revolution.

One year, two classics

Dumas first made his name in the theatre. The novels came later, and quickly: The Three Musketeers began to appear in a newspaper in 1844, and The Count of Monte Cristo started the same year.

Both were written to be read in episodes. That explains their shape: short chapters, a great deal of dialogue, and an ending that makes you want the next issue.

Not alone

Dumas worked with collaborators, the best known being Auguste Maquet, who drafted plots and first versions that Dumas then rewrote. The two ended up in court over money and credit.

A late honour

With his earnings he built the Château de Monte-Cristo, west of Paris, and lost it to his creditors within a few years. He died in 1870. In 2002 his remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris.

item.title: Stendhal, written for later
item.description:
Stendhal is the pen name of Henri Beyle, born in Grenoble in 1783. He followed Napoleon's armies as an administrator, as far as Moscow in 1812, and spent the last part of his career as French consul in Civitavecchia, near Rome. He died in Paris in 1842.

Two novels

Le Rouge et le Noir came out in 1830. It follows Julien Sorel, a carpenter's son who tries to rise in a society that has closed its doors since the fall of Napoleon.

La Chartreuse de Parme followed in 1839. Stendhal dictated it in about seven weeks. Its account of Waterloo, seen by a young man who is never quite sure he was in the battle, became one of its most famous passages.

The happy few

His books sold poorly. He ended the Chartreuse with the words "To the happy few", in English, and said more than once that he would be read much later.

One reader did not wait. In 1840 Balzac published a long and enthusiastic article on the Chartreuse, at a time when few others had noticed it.

A name in medicine

Stendhal described being overwhelmed, almost to the point of fainting, after a visit to the church of Santa Croce in Florence. The reaction of some travellers in front of too much art is now called Stendhal syndrome.

item.title: Liszt and the invention of the recital
item.description:
Franz Liszt was born in 1811 in Raiding, then in the Kingdom of Hungary. He played in public as a child, studied in Vienna, and settled in Paris as a teenager.

One man, one piano

Concerts of the time mixed singers, soloists and an orchestra. Around 1840 Liszt began to give whole evenings by himself, and the word "recital" was used for his London concerts that year. He also played from memory and turned the piano sideways, so that the audience could see his hands.

The effect on the public was strong enough for the poet Heinrich Heine to give it a name: Lisztomania.

After the tours

Liszt stopped touring in his mid-thirties and moved to Weimar in 1848. There he conducted, composed, and wrote orchestral pieces in one movement built on a poem or a painting, which he called symphonic poems. His Piano Sonata in B minor dates from those years.

He also used his position for others, conducting the first performance of Wagner's Lohengrin in 1850. Wagner later married his daughter Cosima.

The abbé

In 1865 Liszt took minor orders in Rome and was known from then on as the Abbé Liszt. He spent his last years between Rome, Weimar and Budapest, teaching without asking for a fee. He died in Bayreuth in 1886.

His years with Marie d'Agoult had already found their way into a novel: Balzac drew on them for Béatrix.

item.title: Saint-Saëns, from the organ to the cinema
item.description:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born in Paris in 1835. He gave his first public concert at the Salle Pleyel in 1846, at the age of ten.

Twenty years at the Madeleine

From 1858 to 1877 he was organist of the church of La Madeleine in Paris, where his improvisations drew visitors. Liszt heard him there and called him the greatest organist in the world.

The two men stayed close. When no Paris theatre wanted the opera Samson et Dalila, Liszt had it staged in Weimar, in 1877. Saint-Saëns dedicated his Third Symphony, the one with organ, to Liszt's memory in 1886.

The piece he kept hidden

The same year he wrote The Carnival of the Animals for a private party. He thought it would harm his reputation as a serious composer and did not allow it to be published in his lifetime, with one exception: The Swan.

It became his most played work after his death.

A first for film

In 1908 he composed the music for L'Assassinat du duc de Guise, a short silent film. It is one of the first scores written for a film by an established composer.

He travelled widely in his last decades and died in Algiers in 1921.
